title: The Real “Mummy’s Curse” Lurks Online
gist: A University of Staffordshire study of 128 social-media and online-auction listings selling mummified human and animal remains found sellers routinely ignore biosecurity risks — chiefly the fungus Aspergillus, historically blamed for 'mummy's curse' deaths — and researchers call for better oversight of the booming online trade.

themes.theme: The historical 'mummy's curse' explained as fungal infection

insights.claim: Howard Carter's 1920s discovery of King Tutankhamun's tomb triggered a wave of 'Tutmania,' and rumors of a 'mummy's curse' spread after his benefactor Lord Carnarvon died of blood poisoning and pneumonia shortly after the tomb's opening.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Establishes the origin of the popular 'mummy's curse' legend that the article goes on to reinterpret through a scientific, infectious-disease lens.
insights.quote: Howard Carter’s discovery of King Tutankhamun’s tomb in the 1920s set off a wave of “Tutmania.” So when his primary benefactor, Lord Carnarvon, dropped dead of blood poisoning and pneumonia shortly after its opening, rumors quickly spread about the “mummy’s curse.”

insights.claim: In 1888, a man named Walter Ingram died at age 33 after purchasing an Egyptian mummy, and half a century after Tutankhamun's tomb was opened, 10 of a dozen conservators who entered Poland's King Casimir IV Jagiellon's tomb died in the following months.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Provides two additional historical death clusters linked to mummy exposure beyond the famous Tutankhamun case, reinforcing the pattern the article attributes to a real biological cause rather than a curse.
insights.quote: In 1888, a man named Walter Ingram died at the age of 33 after purchasing an Egyptian mummy... Half a century after Tut’s tomb was opened, a dozen conservators entered the centuries-old tomb of Poland’s King Casimir IV Jagiellon—in the months that followed 10 of them died.
insights.locator: It wasn't the first time either

insights.claim: The likely culprit behind the historical 'mummy's curse' deaths, including the Casimir IV Jagiellon case, was not a curse but the fungus Aspergillus, whose spores can lay dormant for centuries or millennia and, when inhaled, infect the lungs and produce toxins.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Reframes a centuries-old superstition as a documented infectious-disease risk (fungal spore inhalation), directly relevant to anyone handling ancient organic remains today.
insights.quote: The culprit in that case, and likely the others, wasn’t a curse at all but the fungus Aspergillus. Spores from Aspergillus can lay dormant for centuries—even millennia—and when they’re inhaled they can infect the lungs and produce toxins.

themes.theme: The online trade in mummified remains and its biosecurity risks

insights.claim: A new study in the International Journal of Cultural Property finds that unwary buyers purchasing mummified remains online are at risk of contracting Aspergillus and other pathogens.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Establishes a present-day, quantifiable health risk (not just historical anecdote) tied to the modern online trade in mummified remains.
insights.quote: According to a new study published in the International Journal of Cultural Property, unwary buyers purchasing mummified remains are at risk of contracting this cursed pathogen—and many others.

insights.claim: Bioarchaeologists led by a team from the University of Staffordshire in the UK analyzed 128 posts on Facebook, Instagram, and online auction sites selling mummified remains, finding most listings were for human body parts (hands, feet, and heads especially) alongside mummified animals.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale and composition (128 listings, mostly human body parts) of an active online black-market-adjacent trade in mummified human and animal remains across mainstream social platforms.
insights.quote: Researchers led by a team of bioarchaeologists from the University of Staffordshire in the United Kingdom analyzed 128 posts on Facebook, Instagram, and online auction sites selling mummified remains. Most of the listings were for human body parts (hands, feet, and heads were especially popular), but they also found mummified animals for sale.
insights.locator: Researchers led by a team of bioarchaeologists

insights.claim: Kirsty Squires of the University of Staffordshire said the rise of social media has amplified international trafficking and driven demand for unique cultural heritage items, including mummified humans and animals.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Identifies social media platforms specifically as a demand-driving mechanism behind the illicit trade in cultural heritage and human remains.
insights.quote: “The rise of the internet, especially social media, has amplified international trafficking and driven demand for unique cultural heritage, including mummified humans and animals,” Kirsty Squires of the University of Staffordshire explained in a statement.

insights.claim: Researchers found sellers of mummified remains provided no information about safe handling — some even posted photos of themselves holding specimens with ungloved hands — and several remains showed clear signs of biodeterioration likely caused by fungal activity.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Documents concrete evidence of poor biosecurity practice among online sellers, directly increasing both buyer and seller exposure risk to pathogens like Aspergillus.
insights.quote: Sellers weren’t providing information about safe handling of the specimens (some even posted photos of themselves holding the specimens in ungloved hands). Several of these mummified remains showed clear signs of biodeterioration, likely due to fungal activity.

insights.claim: Beyond fungal spores, chemicals used in ancient embalming practices can also cause skin and lung irritation, and poor storage or packaging by lax sellers could exacerbate fungal activity on mummified remains.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Identifies a second, independent hazard category (embalming chemical residue) beyond fungal spores that buyers and handlers of mummified remains face.
insights.quote: According to the team, fungus isn’t the only biohazard buyers and sellers need to worry about—chemicals used in ancient embalming practices can also cause skin and lung irritation.

insights.claim: Kirsty Squires called for the public to remain vigilant and report sales of mummified remains to relevant authorities and professional bodies, arguing improved oversight and education are essential to safeguard public health and preserve archaeological remains.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete policy/enforcement ask (public reporting plus better oversight and education) as the study's recommended remedy for the identified risks.
insights.quote: “Until more effective measures are implemented, the public should remain vigilant and report sales of mummified remains to relevant authorities and professional bodies,” Squires said. “Improved oversight and education are therefore essential to safeguard public health and preserve archaeological remains.”
